title: Contributing factors, weighted
lede: The weights are our editorial judgment, not a calculation. Click a factor for the evidence.

causes.title: Dependence on phones sold on carriers’ terms
causes.text: Wireless went from 28.7% of sales in 2003 to a 52.4% mobility share in 2013. In 2012 and 2013 the company sold fewer postpaid phones, paid more for each, and repaid commissions when customers dropped service. The 10-K calls the result a “substantial decrease in consolidated gross profit.”[^9][^13]

causes.title: A footprint that never shrank to fit
causes.text: Company stores peaked at 5,289 in 2001 and were still 4,297 at the end of 2013. Apart from 2006, store counts barely moved while sales per store fell by about a fifth between 2005 and 2013 (derived).[^6][^10][^13]

causes.title: The reason to visit moved elsewhere
causes.text: The chain was built on batteries, parts and advice. The archived home pages show the parts business shrinking to a sidebar as phones took over. Online competition is general context; our sources don’t quantify it.[^33]

causes.title: Five chief executives in eight years
causes.text: Edmondson resigned over his résumé in 2006; Day, Gooch and Magnacca followed, each with a new strategy, including “The Shack” in 2009 and the ’80s ad in 2014.[^17][^10][^19][^13]

causes.title: No cushion when it mattered
causes.text: Equity fell from $1,048.3M in 2009 to $206.4M in 2013, and cash from $908.2M to $43.3M by November 2014. There was no room left to close stores in an orderly way.[^13][^14]

disclaimer: How we weight: each factor is scored by how directly the filings tie it to falling gross profit and to the cash drain of 2012–2014. Other analysts could weight these differently.
